1. Lipid Molecules & The Transport Problem

The organizing problem for this entire topic: lipids are hydrophobic, but the intestinal lumen, lymph, and blood are all aqueous environments. Every structure covered in this guide — micelles, chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, HDL — exists to solve this one physical problem.

Why Lipids Matter

  • Cell membranes — phospholipid bilayer
  • Energy storage — triglycerides are the primary dense energy reserve
  • Steroid hormones & signaling — cholesterol is the precursor for all steroid hormones
  • Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E, K absorption depends on normal fat handling

The Five Key Molecules

TermSimple DefinitionPrimary Role
Fatty acidHydrocarbon chainFuel and lipid building block
TriglycerideGlycerol + three fatty acidsEnergy storage and transport
CholesterolFour-ring sterolMembranes and precursor molecule (NOT an energy source)
Cholesterol esterCholesterol + fatty acidHydrophobic transport/storage form (packs into lipoprotein core)
PhospholipidAmphipathic lipidMembranes and lipoprotein surface
Structural comparison: phospholipid vs. fatty acid, and how amphipathic molecules organize into a lipid bilayer or micelle

Cholesterol Synthesis & Homeostasis

  • Body synthesizes ~800–1,000 mg/day, primarily in the liver via HMG-CoA reductase (the rate-limiting, statin-targeted enzyme); dietary intake adds ~300–500 mg/day
  • When dietary cholesterol intake rises, hepatic synthesis falls (and vice versa) — this homeostatic feedback is why dietary cholesterol has a comparatively modest effect on blood cholesterol for most people

Micelle vs. Lipoprotein — Two Solutions, Two Locations

Mixed MicelleLipoprotein
Found in the intestinal lumenFound in lymph and blood
Built with bile saltsBuilt with phospholipids and apolipoproteins
Carries digestion products to the enterocyteCarries packaged lipids between organs
Does NOT enter the enterocyte intactSecreted and transported as an intact particle
Quick test: Where am I? If in the intestinal lumen → think micelle. What's the job? If transporting packaged lipid through blood/lymph → think lipoprotein.

The Pathway We're About to Trace

Meal → stomach → duodenum → emulsified droplet → digestion → micelle → enterocyte → chylomicron → lymph → blood → adipose/muscle → liver
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. A biochemistry lecturer describes a molecule as a four-ring sterol structure that is not used for energy but instead serves as a precursor for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. Which molecule is being described?

Explanation: Cholesterol is fundamentally different from triglycerides — it's a four-ring sterol used structurally (in membranes) and as a precursor for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D, not as an energy source.

2. Which of the following best explains why cholesteryl esters, rather than free cholesterol, are preferentially packed into the core of a lipoprotein particle?

Explanation: Attaching a fatty acid to cholesterol's hydroxyl group creates a cholesteryl ester, which is far more hydrophobic than free cholesterol — allowing it to be densely packed into the hydrophobic core of a lipoprotein, while free (unesterified) cholesterol sits in the amphipathic surface shell.

3. A first-year student is confused about the difference between a mixed micelle and a lipoprotein. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two structures?

Explanation: Mixed micelles solve the hydrophobicity problem in the intestinal lumen using bile salts, and do not enter the enterocyte intact. Lipoproteins solve the same fundamental problem — but in lymph and blood — using a phospholipid/apolipoprotein surface, and they travel as an intact secreted particle.

4. The rate-limiting enzyme for hepatic cholesterol synthesis, and the target of statin medications, is:

Explanation: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis and is the molecular target of statin drugs. (CYP7A1, by contrast, is the rate-limiting enzyme for converting cholesterol into bile acids.)

2. Gastric Phase & CCK Signaling

In the Stomach

  • Mechanical mixing reduces large fat globules into emulsified droplets (true stable emulsification isn't completed until the duodenum, with bile salt help)
  • Gastric lipase (from chief cells) performs only minor triglyceride digestion, at acidic pH
  • Fat slows gastric emptying; most lipid digestion actually occurs in the small intestine

The Signal to the Duodenum: CCK

  • Fat and amino acids in the duodenal lumen stimulate I cells (enteroendocrine cells in duodenum/proximal jejunum) to release cholecystokinin (CCK) into the bloodstream (it's an endocrine hormone, not a luminal secretion)
CCK's four key actions:
  • Gallbladder contraction (expels bile)
  • Sphincter of Oddi relaxation (allows bile + pancreatic juice into the duodenum)
  • Pancreatic enzyme secretion (lipase, colipase, proteases, amylase)
  • Slower gastric emptying (gives the intestine more time to digest/absorb fat)

Why Lipid Handling Requires Multi-Organ Coordination

Organ/SystemContribution
PancreasDigestive enzymes
LiverCholesterol metabolism, bile synthesis
Biliary systemProvides bile salts for micelle formation
Small intestineAbsorption
Muscle & adiposeFuel use & storage
Disorders of excess in this system: MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, formerly NASH), cholecystitis, coronary artery disease, stroke, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K).
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. A researcher studying gastric physiology notes that dietary fat entering the stomach is mechanically churned into smaller droplets. What is the primary purpose of this mechanical mixing?

Explanation: Gastric mechanical mixing reduces large fat globules into smaller emulsified droplets, increasing the surface area available for lipase activity — although true, stable emulsification is completed later in the duodenum with the help of bile salts.

2. Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenal lumen stimulate I cells to release which hormone?

Explanation: Duodenal I cells sense luminal long-chain fatty acids and amino acids/peptides and release CCK into the bloodstream (it is an endocrine hormone, not a luminal secretion).

3. A patient has a condition that impairs CCK release from duodenal I cells after a fatty meal. Which of the following would you expect as a DIRECT consequence?

Explanation: CCK's key actions are gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, pancreatic enzyme secretion, and slowed gastric emptying. Impaired CCK release would blunt bile delivery to the duodenum, in turn impairing fat emulsification.

4. Which enzyme performs a minor amount of triglyceride digestion while food is still in the stomach, well before pancreatic lipase becomes the dominant digestive enzyme?

Explanation: Gastric lipase, secreted by gastric chief cells, performs a minor amount of triglyceride hydrolysis at acidic pH — most lipid digestion occurs later, in the small intestine, via pancreatic lipase.

3. The Biliary System & Bile Salts

  • Bile is synthesized continuously by hepatocytes in the liver
  • Flow path: intrahepatic bile ducts → right/left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct → (between meals) down the cystic duct into the gallbladder
  • The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile 5–20 fold by absorbing water and electrolytes
  • Between meals, the sphincter of Oddi is closed, so bile backs up into the gallbladder; after a meal, CCK triggers gallbladder contraction + sphincter relaxation
The complete picture: peristalsis & release of dietary lipophilic content → emulsification → micellarization → uptake at the enterocyte, with lipolysis detail (bile salts, mono/diglycerides, free fatty acids)

Bile Salts Are Amphipathic

  • Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver (rate-limiting enzyme: cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase, CYP7A1), then conjugated before secretion
  • Their critical property is being amphipathic — interacting with both the hydrophobic lipid and the aqueous lumen
  • First job = emulsification, NOT digestion. Bile salts do not chemically cleave triglycerides — they break a large fat mass into smaller droplets and keep them dispersed, giving pancreatic enzymes far more surface area to act on

Anatomy Refresher

Liver produces bile → gallbladder stores/concentrates it → pancreas produces digestive enzymes → both converge at the duodenum, which receives bile (for the physical hydrophobicity problem) and pancreatic enzymes (for the chemical digestion problem) at essentially the same location. A blockage anywhere along this system can disrupt fat digestion.

📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. Bile is continuously synthesized by which cell type?

Explanation: Hepatocytes in the liver continuously synthesize bile, which then flows through the intrahepatic ducts, the right/left hepatic ducts, the common hepatic duct, and (between meals) down the cystic duct into the gallbladder for storage.

2. Between meals, the sphincter of Oddi is closed. What happens to bile during this period?

Explanation: With the sphincter of Oddi closed between meals, bile backs up into the gallbladder, which concentrates it 5- to 20-fold by absorbing water and electrolytes, until CCK triggers gallbladder contraction and sphincter relaxation after a meal.

3. What is the primary initial function of bile salts when they contact a large dietary fat globule in the duodenum?

Explanation: Bile salts are amphipathic and do not chemically cleave triglycerides — that's pancreatic lipase's job. Their first role is emulsification: coating fat droplets, preventing them from recoalescing, and dramatically increasing surface area for enzymatic digestion.

4. A patient with a biliary obstruction has markedly reduced bile salt delivery to the intestine, but pancreatic lipase secretion remains completely normal. Which best describes the expected outcome?

Explanation: Even with intact lipase activity, without bile salts the products of lipolysis cannot form mixed micelles and cross the unstirred water layer efficiently — leading to steatorrhea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. The defect here is solubilization/delivery, not hydrolysis.

4. Pancreatic Digestion & Micelle Formation

Fat globule → emulsified fat droplets (via bile salt mechanical/amphipathic action) → micelles (via pancreatic lipase + colipase) → mixed micelle → absorption across the brush border

Pancreatic Enzymes Act at the Lipid-Water Interface

  • Pancreatic lipase + colipase: hydrolyze triglycerides → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 free fatty acids. Colipase anchors lipase to the droplet surface, increasing turnover ~10–15×
  • Cholesterol esterase: cholesterol esters → free cholesterol + fatty acids
  • Phospholipase A2: phospholipids → lysophospholipids + fatty acids

Mixed Micelle Formation

  • As digestion products accumulate, they associate with bile salts to form mixed micelles — hydrophilic exterior (bile salts), hydrophobic core (monoglycerides, free fatty acids, cholesterol, lysophospholipids, fat-soluble vitamins)
  • Micelles are necessary because these products are poorly soluble in the aqueous lumen and would otherwise diffuse extremely slowly across the unstirred water layer at the brush border
  • Bile salts themselves remain in the lumen for enterohepatic recirculation — they are not absorbed with the lipid cargo

Component Checkpoint Table

ComponentSourceFunctionHigh-Yield Detail
Gastric lipaseChief cells (stomach)Minor TG hydrolysisAcidic pH; minor vs. pancreatic lipase
CCKI-cells (duodenum/jejunum)GB contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, pancreatic secretionReleased in response to fats/amino acids
Bile saltsHepatocytes (from cholesterol)Emulsification → micelle formationRate-limiting enzyme: CYP7A1
Pancreatic lipase + colipasePancreatic acinar cellsCleaves TG → 2-MAG + 2 FFAsColipase ↑turnover ~10–15×
NPC1L1Enterocyte brush borderActive cholesterol absorptionTarget of ezetimibe
What happens if micelles can't form? Absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and lipids is greatly diminished — even if lipase is hydrolyzing triglycerides normally, the products can't efficiently cross the unstirred water layer without micelles.
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. Pancreatic lipase requires which cofactor to anchor it to the lipid droplet surface and allow efficient triglyceride hydrolysis?

Explanation: Colipase anchors pancreatic lipase to the lipid droplet surface, increasing its turnover roughly 10- to 15-fold; without colipase, lipase cannot efficiently access triglycerides within the droplet.

2. Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes a triglyceride into which products?

Explanation: Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) hydrolyzes triglyceride into 2-monoacylglycerol plus two free fatty acids — it does not fully hydrolyze the molecule down to free glycerol.

3. Which enzyme converts cholesterol esters into free cholesterol and fatty acids within the intestinal lumen, allowing the products to enter mixed micelles?

Explanation: Cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes dietary cholesterol esters into free cholesterol and fatty acids in the intestinal lumen, allowing the products to be incorporated into mixed micelles for delivery to the enterocyte.

4. A mixed micelle in the intestinal lumen is primarily composed of which combination of molecules?

Explanation: Mixed micelles are composed of bile salts (forming the hydrophilic exterior) surrounding fatty acids, monoacylglycerol, cholesterol, lysophospholipids, and fat-soluble vitamins in the hydrophobic interior — allowing these poorly water-soluble digestion products to cross the unstirred water layer to the enterocyte.

5. Absorption & Chylomicron Assembly

Crossing the Brush Border

Digestion ProductAbsorption Mechanism
Free fatty acids & 2-monoacylglycerolPassive diffusion (no energy required)
Free cholesterolEnergy-dependent uptake via NPC1L1
Board pharmacology correlation: Ezetimibe (Zetia) inhibits NPC1L1, selectively reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption. Someone with high cholesterol given this drug would have reduced cholesterol entering the enterocyte.

Inside the Enterocyte: Reassembly

  • Free fatty acids + monoacylglycerol are reassembled into triglycerides in the smooth ER
  • Free cholesterol is re-esterified back into cholesterol ester
  • Why digest something just to rebuild it? Digestion was necessary only to cross the intestinal barrier. Once inside, the cell wants these molecules back in their highly hydrophobic transport form so they can be packaged into a lipoprotein.
  • ApoB-48 is synthesized and, together with the reassembled lipids, forms the nascent chylomicron

Chylomicron Structure

Chylomicron: ~0.1–1 µm, ~84% triglyceride core, with surface ApoB-48 (structural), and later-acquired ApoC-II/ApoC-III
  • Assembly requires MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) to lipidate ApoB-48 — the same enzyme lipidates ApoB-100 in the liver for VLDL assembly
  • Chylomicrons are processed through the Golgi, transported to the basolateral membrane, and released by exocytosis into the lamina propria
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. Free fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol cross the enterocyte brush border primarily by which mechanism?

Explanation: Free fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol are small enough and sufficiently lipophilic to cross the apical enterocyte membrane by passive diffusion, unlike cholesterol, which requires the NPC1L1 transporter.

2. A cholesterol-lowering medication works by inhibiting the intestinal transporter responsible for cholesterol uptake into enterocytes. This drug is:

Explanation: Ezetimibe selectively inhibits NPC1L1, the transporter responsible for energy-dependent cholesterol uptake at the enterocyte brush border, thereby reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption.

3. Once inside the enterocyte, free fatty acids and monoacylglycerol are reassembled into triglycerides, and free cholesterol is re-esterified. What is the purpose of this reassembly process?

Explanation: Digestion (hydrolysis) was necessary only to allow the lipid components to cross the intestinal barrier. Once inside the enterocyte, the fatty acids/monoacylglycerol are reassembled into triglycerides and cholesterol is re-esterified — recreating highly hydrophobic forms suitable for packaging into a chylomicron for transport.

4. Which apolipoprotein forms the essential structural scaffold of a newly assembled chylomicron within the enterocyte?

Explanation: ApoB-48 is synthesized in the enterocyte and provides the essential structural scaffold for the nascent chylomicron; it is a truncated version of the same gene product that becomes ApoB-100 in the liver, but lacks ApoB-100's LDL-receptor-binding domain.

6. Exogenous Pathway: Chylomicron Transport

Why Lymph, Not Blood, First?

Because of their large size (up to ~1,200 nm), chylomicrons cannot cross into intestinal blood capillaries. Instead: lacteal → lymphatic vessels → cisterna chyli → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein → systemic circulation. This means dietary long-chain triglyceride initially bypasses hepatic first-pass processing.

The Full Pathway

  1. Chylomicron built in enterocyte with ApoB-48, secreted into lacteals, travels through lymph, enters blood via the thoracic duct
  2. Acquires ApoC-II and ApoE from HDL (HDL acts as a circulating reservoir of exchangeable apolipoproteins)
  3. ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase (LPL), anchored on capillary endothelium (via GPIHBP1) in adipose tissue and muscle
  4. LPL hydrolyzes chylomicron triglycerides → releases free fatty acids → delivered to tissue
  5. Adipose re-esterifies and stores fatty acids as triglyceride; muscle (skeletal & cardiac) oxidizes them for ATP via β-oxidation
A single palmitate molecule yields ~106 ATP via β-oxidation — far more energy per molecule than glucose. This is why the heart, which never rests, derives 60–70% of its energy from fatty acid oxidation.

ApoC-II vs. ApoC-III: The Accelerator and the Brake

  • ApoC-II = accelerator — activates LPL, unlocks triglyceride delivery
  • ApoC-III = brake — opposes LPL activity, slows remnant clearance
  • The balance between the two on a particle's surface determines how quickly it's processed

The HDL Exchange (Bidirectional!)

  • As LPL strips triglyceride, the chylomicron shrinks; its surface phospholipid/free cholesterol becomes relatively excess and is shed onto HDL — one major way HDL acquires cholesterol (not just scavenging arterial walls)
  • CETP simultaneously swaps HDL's cholesteryl esters for the chylomicron's triglycerides

Remnant Clearance

  • After triglyceride removal, the particle becomes smaller and relatively cholesterol-enriched = chylomicron remnant
  • ApoC-II/ApoC-III return to HDL; ApoE remains on the remnant and is recognized by hepatic LDL receptor and LRP1 for receptor-mediated endocytosis
  • Why ApoE matters: ApoB-48 lacks the receptor-binding domain that ApoB-100 has, so without borrowed ApoE, the liver has no efficient way to clear chylomicron remnants
  • Delivered cholesterol suppresses hepatic HMG-CoA reductase (less need for the liver to synthesize its own) — a key homeostatic feedback loop
Apolipoprotein job summary: ApoB-48 builds the chylomicron. ApoC-II unloads triglyceride via LPL. ApoE gets the remnant home to the liver.
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. Why do newly formed chylomicrons enter the lymphatic lacteals rather than the intestinal blood capillaries directly?

Explanation: Chylomicrons are enormous compared to most circulating particles (up to ~1,200 nm), so they cannot enter the fenestrated blood capillaries directly — instead they enter the lymphatic lacteals and travel via the thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein.

2. After a chylomicron enters the bloodstream, it acquires ApoC-II and ApoE from which source?

Explanation: HDL serves as a circulating reservoir of exchangeable apolipoproteins. It transfers ApoC-II and ApoE onto the chylomicron once the chylomicron is in the bloodstream — the same donation occurs for VLDL in the endogenous pathway.

3. Which apolipoprotein acts as the essential cofactor that activates lipoprotein lipase (LPL) on the capillary endothelium of muscle and adipose tissue?

Explanation: ApoC-II is the obligate cofactor that activates LPL, allowing it to hydrolyze the triglycerides carried within the chylomicron core and release free fatty acids to the underlying tissue.

4. As lipoprotein lipase progressively removes triglyceride from a circulating chylomicron, the particle becomes smaller and its excess surface phospholipid and free cholesterol are transferred to HDL. What is the resulting particle called, and what apolipoprotein guides its hepatic clearance?

Explanation: After LPL removes most of the triglyceride, the resulting smaller, relatively cholesterol-enriched particle is called a chylomicron remnant. ApoE (which the particle retains after ApoC-II/ApoC-III return to HDL) is recognized by hepatic receptors (LDL receptor and LRP1), enabling receptor-mediated hepatic uptake.

7. Endogenous Pathway: VLDL → IDL → LDL

VLDL: The Liver's Export Vehicle

  • Liver packages triglycerides + cholesterol with a single ApoB-100 molecule per particle — this is why plasma ApoB-100 reflects the number of atherogenic particles, not just how much lipid they carry
  • VLDL triglyceride sources: (1) albumin-bound FFAs delivered to the liver, or from remnant uptake, and (2) fatty acids the liver makes itself via de novo lipogenesis
  • If the liver makes/receives more triglyceride than it can export as VLDL, triglyceride accumulates in hepatocytes → hepatic steatosis
Lifecycle of a single ApoB-100 particle: liver secretes VLDL → LPL removes triglyceride → VLDL remnant → LDL. VLDL-to-LDL conversion takes ~6 hours; LDL circulates ~48 hours total (spending ~90% of its lifecycle as LDL). Particles <70nm can cross the endothelial barrier and become trapped in the arterial wall, driving atherosclerotic plaque formation.

The Same Machinery, Reused

  • VLDL acquires ApoC-II and ApoE from HDL — identical to the chylomicron exchange
  • ApoC-II activates LPL → hydrolyzes VLDL triglyceride → releases FFAs to muscle (oxidation) and adipose (storage)
  • As VLDL loses triglyceride, it becomes IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein)

IDL's Two Fates

  • Fate 1: Taken back up by the liver via ApoE-mediated binding to hepatic LDL receptors/LRP (same remnant-clearance machinery as chylomicrons)
  • Fate 2: Loses further triglyceride (partly via hepatic lipase) → becomes LDL

LDL: The Cholesterol Delivery End-Product

  • LDL has lost most of its triglyceride and is now relatively enriched in cholesteryl ester; its job is delivering cholesterol to peripheral cells
  • ApoB-100 on LDL binds the LDL receptor → receptor-mediated endocytosis; ~70% of circulating LDL is cleared by hepatic LDL receptors
LDL particle structure: a single ApoB-100 wraps a phospholipid monolayer shell around a core of cholesteryl esters and triacylglycerol, with free cholesterol interspersed in the surface layer

PCSK9: The Master Regulator of LDL Receptor Fate

  • Normally, after the LDL receptor delivers LDL into the hepatocyte, the receptor separates and recycles back to the surface
  • PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor and redirects it to lysosomal degradation instead of recycling
↑PCSK9 → ↓LDL receptors → ↓LDL clearance → ↑plasma LDL
PCSK9 inhibition → ↑LDL receptors → ↑LDL clearance → ↓plasma LDL
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. The liver packages triglycerides and cholesterol into VLDL using which structural apolipoprotein, present as a single copy per particle?

Explanation: The liver assembles VLDL around a single ApoB-100 molecule per particle. Because each particle carries exactly one ApoB-100, plasma ApoB-100 concentration reflects the NUMBER of circulating atherogenic particles, not simply how much lipid they carry.

2. As VLDL loses triglyceride via LPL-mediated hydrolysis, it is progressively converted first to IDL and then to LDL. Which statement about this transition is correct?

Explanation: IDL has two possible fates: some is cleared by the liver via ApoE-mediated binding to hepatic LDL receptors/LRP (the same remnant-clearance machinery used for chylomicron remnants), while the rest loses additional triglyceride (partly via hepatic lipase) to become LDL.

3. A patient is found to have a gain-of-function mutation in PCSK9. What is the expected effect on LDL receptor availability and plasma LDL-C?

Explanation: PCSK9 normally binds the LDL receptor and directs it toward lysosomal degradation instead of recycling. A gain-of-function mutation accelerates this degradation, reducing the number of LDL receptors available on hepatocytes, impairing LDL clearance, and raising plasma LDL-C — a recognized cause of autosomal dominant familial hypercholesterolemia.

4. Approximately what proportion of circulating LDL is cleared by hepatic LDL receptors under normal physiologic conditions?

Explanation: The liver is the major site of LDL clearance, accounting for roughly 70% of circulating LDL removal via hepatic LDL receptors — which is why hepatic LDL receptor number/activity is such a major determinant of plasma LDL-C.

8. HDL & Reverse Cholesterol Transport

Mammalian cells cannot break down cholesterol's steroid ring, so any excess cholesterol accumulating in peripheral cells has to be moved elsewhere. This is reverse cholesterol transport, and HDL is the central vehicle.

Reverse cholesterol transport: macrophage cholesterol efflux (ABCA1/ABCG1) → nascent pre-β-HDL → LCAT esterification → mature α-HDL → direct pathway (SR-B1) or indirect pathway (CETP) to the liver

Step-by-Step

  1. ApoA-I (made in liver/intestine, initially lipid-poor) accepts phospholipids and free cholesterol from cells via the ABCA1 transporter → forms nascent (pre-β) HDL
  2. LCAT (activated by ApoA-I) esterifies free cholesterol → cholesteryl ester moves into the HDL core → HDL matures into α-HDL
  3. Mature HDL can continue accepting cholesterol from macrophages via ABCG1

Two Routes Back to the Liver

PathwayMechanism
DirectHDL binds hepatic SR-B1, which selectively extracts cholesteryl ester without destroying the HDL particle — HDL is remodeled and reused
IndirectCETP transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL/IDL/LDL in exchange for triglycerides; those ApoB-containing particles are then cleared via the LDL receptor
Clinical consequence of CETP in hypertriglyceridemic states: CETP-mediated exchange depletes HDL of cholesterol while loading it with triglyceride → smaller, denser HDL particles cleared more rapidly → explains why high triglycerides and low HDL-C so often travel together. The same CETP action loads LDL with triglyceride, which hepatic lipase then strips, producing small dense LDL — the classic metabolic syndrome lipid pattern.

Putting It All Together

Exogenous (dietary, chylomicron-based) vs. endogenous (hepatic, VLDL-based) pathways side by side — both converge on LPL-mediated fatty acid delivery to adipose/muscle, and both feed into the shared HDL/LCAT system for returning cholesterol to the liver
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. Nascent HDL is formed when lipid-poor ApoA-I accepts phospholipids and free cholesterol from peripheral cells via which transporter?

Explanation: ABCA1 transfers phospholipids and free cholesterol from cells (such as macrophages) onto lipid-poor ApoA-I, forming nascent (pre-β) HDL — the first step of reverse cholesterol transport.

2. Which enzyme, activated by ApoA-I, esterifies free cholesterol on the surface of nascent HDL so that it can move into the particle's hydrophobic core as HDL matures?

Explanation: LCAT, activated by ApoA-I, esterifies free cholesterol into cholesteryl ester, allowing it to move into the hydrophobic core of the maturing HDL particle — converting nascent (pre-β) HDL into mature (α) HDL.

3. Mature HDL can deliver cholesteryl ester directly back to the liver via which receptor, without requiring degradation of the entire HDL particle?

Explanation: SR-B1 selectively extracts cholesteryl ester from HDL at the liver without destroying the HDL particle itself, allowing HDL to be remodeled and continue participating in further rounds of cholesterol transport (the 'direct' pathway of reverse cholesterol transport).

4. Which plasma protein mediates the 'indirect' pathway of reverse cholesterol transport by exchanging cholesteryl esters from HDL for triglycerides from VLDL, IDL, or LDL?

Explanation: CETP transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to ApoB-containing lipoproteins (VLDL/IDL/LDL) in exchange for triglycerides. Those ApoB-containing particles are then cleared by the liver via the LDL receptor — the 'indirect' route for returning cholesterol to the liver.

9. Disorders of the Exogenous Pathway

Pattern to notice: defects before the enterocyte (bile salts, lipase) cause malabsorption + ADEK vitamin deficiency. Defects at export (ApoB-48/MTP) cause malabsorption despite normal digestion. Defects after secretion (LPL/ApoC-II, ApoE) cause hyperlipidemias.
DefectNamed ConditionKey Features
Bile salts can't reach intestine (biliary obstruction, cholestasis, ileal resection)—↓emulsification/micelles → steatorrhea + ADEK deficiency. Lipase still works — defect is solubilization, not hydrolysis
Pancreatic lipase absent (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis)—Steatorrhea appears only once lipase output drops to ~5–10% of normal (large functional reserve)
MTP defect — can't lipidate ApoB in enterocyte or hepatocyteAbetalipoproteinemiaNear-absent ApoB-lipoproteins, extremely low LDL-C/TG, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa, spinocerebellar ataxia (fat-soluble vitamin loss)
ApoC-II or LPL deficient (or GPIHBP1, ApoA-V, LMF1)Type I familial chylomicronemia syndromeTG often >1,000 mg/dL, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent pancreatitis. ASCVD risk NOT increased (low ApoB particle number)
ApoE can't bind hepatic receptors (ApoE2/E2)Type III familial dysbetalipoproteinemiaRoughly equal ↑cholesterol + ↑TG, palmar & tuberoeruptive xanthomas, premature ASCVD. Only 10–15% of ApoE2/E2 homozygotes express phenotype — needs a 2nd metabolic hit
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. An infant presents with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, and acanthocytosis. Laboratory testing reveals near-absent chylomicrons, extremely low LDL-C, and extremely low triglycerides. Genetic testing reveals a defect in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP). Which condition is this?

Explanation: Abetalipoproteinemia results from MTP defects, which prevent lipidation of ApoB in both enterocytes (chylomicron assembly) and hepatocytes (VLDL assembly). This causes near-absent ApoB-containing lipoproteins, extremely low LDL-C/triglycerides, fat malabsorption, and — due to fat-soluble vitamin deficiency — retinitis pigmentosa, spinocerebellar ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy, plus acanthocytosis.

2. A young adult presents with triglycerides over 1,000 mg/dL, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and recurrent pancreatitis. Plasma develops a creamy supernatant on standing. This presentation is most consistent with a defect in which protein(s)?

Explanation: This is Type I familial chylomicronemia syndrome, classically caused by LPL deficiency or ApoC-II deficiency (its obligate cofactor) — chylomicrons are secreted but cannot be efficiently hydrolyzed, leading to massive TG-rich particle accumulation. Note that ASCVD risk is generally NOT increased here because ApoB particle number is low.

3. A patient with ApoE2/E2 homozygosity develops palmar xanthomas, tuberoeruptive xanthomas, and roughly equal elevations in both cholesterol and triglycerides, following the onset of new hypothyroidism. This presentation is most consistent with:

Explanation: Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia results from impaired ApoE binding to hepatic remnant receptors (classically ApoE2/E2), causing accumulation of chylomicron remnants and IDL, with roughly proportional elevation of cholesterol and triglycerides, and characteristic palmar/tuberoeruptive xanthomas. Only ~10–15% of ApoE2/E2 homozygotes express the phenotype — a second metabolic 'hit' (like this patient's new hypothyroidism) is typically required.

4. What is the key laboratory/clinical distinction that helps differentiate Type I familial chylomicronemia syndrome (LPL/ApoC-II deficiency) from Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia (ApoE2/E2)?

Explanation: Type I (LPL/ApoC-II deficiency) causes massive, isolated triglyceride elevation (often >1,000 mg/dL) with LOW ApoB particle number and therefore low ASCVD risk. Type III (ApoE2/E2) causes accumulation of cholesterol-rich remnants and IDL, with roughly proportional elevation of both cholesterol and triglycerides, and IS associated with premature atherosclerosis.

10. Disorders of the Endogenous Pathway

DefectNamed ConditionKey Features
Liver overproduces VLDLType IV familial hypertriglyceridemia↑VLDL/TG (often 200–500 mg/dL), ↓HDL-C, ApoB not markedly elevated. Common (5–10% prevalence); linked to obesity/insulin resistance/alcohol
Liver overproduces both VLDL and ApoB-100Type IIb familial combined hyperlipidemia (FCHL)↑ApoB with VARIABLE expression (some high LDL-C, some high TG, some both) across family members; small dense LDL common; one of the most common inherited dyslipidemias (~1–2%)
LDL receptor cannot clear LDLType IIa familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)Markedly ↑LDL-C (heterozygous ≥190 mg/dL, homozygous often >500), normal TG, tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus, premature ASCVD/early MI
PCSK9 gain-of-functionAutosomal dominant FH phenocopyAccelerated LDL receptor degradation → ↑LDL-C, resembling classic FH
PCSK9 loss-of-function—↑LDL receptor recycling → ↓LDL-C; lifelong carriers have substantially ↓coronary heart disease risk (rationale for evolocumab/alirocumab)
Insulin no longer suppresses adipose lipolysisMetabolic syndrome / T2DM dyslipidemia"Atherogenic triad": ↑TG, ↓HDL-C, small dense LDL
Similar phenotypes to FH can also arise from defective ApoB-100 itself (familial defective ApoB, can't bind the receptor) or LDLRAP1 defects (receptor can't internalize) — three different molecular lesions converging on the same clinical picture.
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. A patient with obesity and insulin resistance is found to have elevated VLDL and triglycerides (commonly 200–500 mg/dL) with low HDL-C, but ApoB is not markedly elevated. This pattern is most consistent with:

Explanation: Type IV familial hypertriglyceridemia results from hepatic VLDL overproduction, causing elevated VLDL/triglycerides (often 200–500 mg/dL) with low HDL-C, but without the marked ApoB elevation characteristic of Type IIb FCHL. It's common (5–10% prevalence) and strongly linked to obesity, insulin resistance, and alcohol use.

2. A family has several members with dyslipidemia: one relative has isolated high LDL-C, another has isolated high triglycerides, and a third has both elevated. All affected members share an elevated ApoB level. This pattern, with variable phenotypic expression but consistently elevated ApoB, describes:

Explanation: Familial combined hyperlipidemia (Type IIb) is characterized by elevated ApoB (reflecting an increased number of atherogenic particles) with VARIABLE expression across family members — some predominantly high LDL-C, others high triglycerides, others both — and small dense LDL is common. It's one of the most common inherited dyslipidemias (~1-2% prevalence).

3. A patient started on a PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab) for hypercholesterolemia asks how the medication works. Which explanation is correct?

Explanation: PCSK9 inhibitors block PCSK9, which normally directs the LDL receptor toward lysosomal degradation after it delivers LDL to the hepatocyte. By inhibiting PCSK9, more LDL receptors are recycled back to the cell surface, enhancing LDL clearance and lowering plasma LDL-C — the same physiologic effect seen naturally in patients with PCSK9 loss-of-function mutations, who have a lifelong reduction in coronary heart disease risk.

4. In poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, loss of insulin's normal antilipolytic effect on adipose tissue leads to which downstream lipid pattern?

Explanation: Loss of insulin's antilipolytic effect disinhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing FFA release from adipose tissue. This drives increased hepatic VLDL production, and insulin deficiency also reduces LPL activity (LPL is insulin-induced) — the combination produces the classic 'atherogenic triad': hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL-C, and small dense LDL seen in metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes.

11. Disorders of HDL & Reverse Cholesterol Transport

DefectNamed ConditionKey Features
ABCA1 mutated — can't form nascent HDLTangier diseaseNear-absent HDL-C; cholesteryl esters accumulate in macrophages/reticuloendothelial tissue → enlarged orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, corneal opacities. Autosomal recessive
LCAT mutatedFamilial LCAT deficiency (FLD) / Fish-eye disease (FED)Very low HDL-C. FLD (near-complete loss): corneal opacities + hemolytic anemia/acanthocytosis + proteinuria/renal disease. FED (partial loss): corneal opacities only, no renal disease
SR-B1 mutated—HDL-C rises paradoxically because HDL can't efficiently deliver cholesterol to liver — reverse cholesterol transport is actually impaired despite high HDL-C. CV risk not necessarily reduced
CETP mutated—Markedly ↑HDL-C (sometimes >100 mg/dL); well-described in Japanese populations. Relationship to CV outcomes is complex — CETP inhibitor drug trials had mixed results, so don't assume "more HDL = protective"
Big picture takeaway: A high HDL-C number does not automatically mean cardioprotection (see SR-B1 and CETP deficiency) — what matters is whether reverse cholesterol transport is actually functioning, not just the lab value.
📝 Check Your Understanding (4 questions)

1. A patient presents with enlarged orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, corneal opacities, and near-absent HDL-C. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in ABCA1. This condition is:

Explanation: Tangier disease results from ABCA1 mutations, preventing the transfer of phospholipids/free cholesterol onto ApoA-I to form nascent HDL. This causes near-absent HDL-C, with cholesteryl esters accumulating in reticuloendothelial tissue — producing the classic enlarged orange tonsils, along with hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, and corneal opacities.

2. A patient with very low HDL-C is found to have corneal opacities and hemolytic anemia with acanthocytosis, along with proteinuria and progressive renal disease. Which enzyme deficiency best explains this presentation?

Explanation: Familial LCAT deficiency (a near-complete loss of LCAT activity) causes very low HDL-C along with corneal opacities, hemolytic anemia with acanthocytosis, proteinuria, and progressive renal disease. A partial-activity variant, fish-eye disease, causes corneal opacities without the renal involvement.

3. A patient is found to have paradoxically elevated HDL-C but impaired reverse cholesterol transport, because HDL cannot efficiently deliver cholesteryl esters to hepatocytes. This is most consistent with dysfunction of which receptor?

Explanation: SR-B1 normally allows the liver to selectively extract cholesteryl esters from HDL without destroying the particle. If SR-B1 is dysfunctional, HDL cannot efficiently deliver cholesterol to the liver — HDL-C rises paradoxically even though reverse cholesterol transport is actually impaired, illustrating that a high HDL-C number does not always indicate cardioprotection.

4. Which statement about CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein) deficiency is most accurate?

Explanation: CETP deficiency (well described in Japanese populations) causes markedly elevated HDL-C, sometimes above 100 mg/dL. However, its relationship to cardiovascular outcomes is genuinely complex — pharmaceutical CETP inhibitor trials produced mixed cardiovascular results, so this should not be memorized as a simple 'more HDL = more protection' scenario.
